note.note:
History:
- Main complaint: Wheezing with shortness of breath.
- Onset/duration: Began ~2 days ago after house cleaning with significant dust exposure; wheeze started about an hour after cleaning.
- Course/progression: Getting worse over the past 2 days; worse at night.
- Severity/impact: Sometimes unable to complete sentences while talking; feels short of breath.
- Associated symptoms: Denies chest pain with deep breaths; denies dizziness.
- Context: Has not taken any medication for this episode. No antihistamines at home. Drinking fluids adequately. Able to travel to a nearby GP clinic within minutes by car.

Past Medical History:
- Childhood asthma; occasional exercise-induced symptoms as an adult.
- Seasonal hay fever (summer).
- Prior oral steroids for asthma (details not documented).
- Medications: Has an asthma inhaler from a few months ago (type/dose/route/frequency not documented); not currently using it for this episode.
- Allergies: No known allergies reported.
- Regular care: Does not see a doctor regularly for asthma.
- Smoking, family history, hospitalizations, surgical history: Not recorded.

Physical Examination:
- Objective vitals/exam: Not recorded (remote consult; video lost during call).
- Relevant negatives: No chest pain with deep inspiration; no dizziness reported.
- General: Able to converse during call, though reports intermittent difficulty completing sentences at times outside the call.

Impression:
- Suspected acute asthma exacerbation likely triggered by dust/allergen exposure, with nocturnal worsening and dyspnea.
- DDx (consistent with transcript):
  - Irritant-induced bronchospasm from dust exposure: plausible given timing after cleaning.
  - Allergic rhinitis with lower-airway involvement: possible given history of hay fever, though nasal symptoms not reported.

Management Plan:
- In-person evaluation advised at GP/clinic today.
- Test: Pulse oximetry (finger device) to assess oxygen saturation; further assessment as per GP.
- Medication advice: Consider taking an over-the-counter antihistamine en route if available; if not, GP can prescribe.
- Steroids: May be needed depending on in-person assessment (to be decided after evaluation).
- Documentation: Letter to GP provided via app summarizing this consult.
- Safety: No specific red-flag counseling documented in transcript.

Patient Summary:
- 40-year-old with history of childhood asthma and seasonal hay fever developed wheeze and shortness of breath after heavy dust exposure during house cleaning, worsening over 2 days and at night.
- Presentation consistent with an acute asthma exacerbation versus irritant/allergic bronchospasm.
- Plan is urgent same-day GP assessment with pulse oximetry and consideration of antihistamine; steroids may be required pending evaluation.

Key Takeaways:
- Seek same-day in-person GP evaluation for worsening wheeze/shortness of breath.
- Obtain and take an OTC antihistamine if possible on the way; otherwise GP can prescribe.
- Expect a brief visit; a referral letter has been sent via the app.

Next Steps:
- Attend GP/clinic for pulse oximetry and clinical assessment today.
- Follow GP recommendations, which may include medications (e.g., antihistamine and/or steroids) based on findings.
- Monitor symptoms and follow up as directed by GP.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: Vitals (RR, HR, BP, SpO2), peak flow or spirometry, detailed respiratory exam, full review of systems (cough, fever, rhinorrhea, chest tightness), smoking status, medication specifics (inhaler type/dose/frequency), exact travel time, allergy specifics (drug vs environmental), pregnancy status not applicable/not asked.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted.
- Transcript quality: Some audio/video loss and incomplete phrases; no objective measurements obtained during call.
